entries.f10cd87f1c1ce9bba82db1a0bbb2630c50b1a725: <div sID="gen11963" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="82" osisID="Ps.82" sID="Ps.82"/> <div eID="gen11963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11964" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11965" type="x-p"/> This psalm is calculated for the meridian of princes' courts and courts of justice, not in Israel only, but in other nations; yet it was probably penned primarily for the use of the magistrates of Israel, the great Sanhedrim, and their other elders who were in places of power, and perhaps by David's direction. This psalm is designed to make kings wise, and "to instruct the judges of the earth" (as <reference osisRef="Ps.82.2">2</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.82.10">10</reference>), to tell them their duty as (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.3">2 Sam. xxiii. 3</reference>), and to tell them of their faults as <reference osisRef="Ps.58.1">Ps. lviii. 1</reference>. We have here, I. The dignity of magistracy and its dependence upon God, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.1">ver. 1</reference>. II. The duty of magistrates, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.3-Ps.82.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. III. The degeneracy of bad magistrates and the mischief they do, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.2">ver. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">5</reference>. IV. Their doom read, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.6-Ps.82.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. V. The desire and prayer of all good people that the kingdom of God may be set up more and more, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.8">ver. 8</reference>. Though magistrates may most closely apply this psalm to themselves, yet we may any of us sing it with understanding when we give glory to God, in singing it, as presiding in all public affairs, providing for the protection of injured innocency, and ready to punish the most powerful injustice, and when we comfort ourselves with a belief of his present government and with the hopes of his future judgment.
entries.da5dfc55cb9bac94e5b3629a27fe93cf6482ec61: <div eID="gen11965" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11964" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Duty of Magistrates.</title> <div sID="gen11966" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods. <hi type="super">2</hi> How long will ye judge unjustly, and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah. <hi type="super">3</hi> Defend the poor and fatherless: do justice to the afflicted and needy. <hi type="super">4</hi> Deliver the poor and needy: rid <hi type="italic">them</hi> out of the hand of the wicked. <hi type="super">5</hi> They know not, neither will they understand; they walk on in darkness: all the foundations of the earth are out of course. <div eID="gen11966" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11967" type="x-p"/> We have here, <div eID="gen11967" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11968" type="x-p"/> I. God's supreme presidency and power in all councils and courts asserted and laid down, as a great truth necessary to be believed both by princes and subjects (<reference osisRef="Ps.82.1">v. 1</reference>): <hi type="italic">God stands,</hi> as chief director, <hi type="italic">in the congregation of the mighty,</hi> the mighty One, <hi type="italic">in coetu fortis—in the councils of the prince,</hi> the supreme magistrate, and he judges among the gods, the inferior magistrates; both the legislative and the executive power of princes is under his eye and his hand. Observe here, 1. The power and honour of magistrates; they are the <hi type="italic">mighty.</hi> They are so in authority, for the public good (it is a great power that they are entrusted with), and they ought to be so in wisdom and courage. They are, in the Hebrew dialect, called <hi type="italic">gods;</hi> the same word is used for these subordinate governors that is used for the sovereign ruler of the world. They are <hi type="italic">elohim.</hi> Angels are so called both because they are great in power and might and because God is pleased to make use of their service in the government of this lower world; and magistrates in an inferior capacity are likewise the ministers of his providence in general, for the keeping up of order and peace in human societies, and particularly of his justice and goodness in punishing evil-doers and protecting those that do well. Good magistrates, who answer the ends of magistracy, are as God; some of his honour is put upon them; they are his vicegerents, and great blessings to any people. <hi type="italic">A divine sentence is in the lips of the king,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.16.10">Prov. xvi. 10</reference>. But, as <hi type="italic">roaring lions and ranging bears,</hi> so are <hi type="italic">wicked rulers over the poor people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.28.15">Prov. xxviii. 15</reference>. 2. A good form and constitution of government intimated, and that is a mixed monarchy like ours; here is the mighty One, the Sovereign, and here is his congregation, his privy-council, his parliament, his bench of judges, who are called the <hi type="italic">gods.</hi> 3. God's incontestable sovereignty maintained in and over all the congregations of the mighty. <hi type="italic">God stands,</hi> he <hi type="italic">judges among them;</hi> they have their power from him and are accountable to him. <hi type="italic">By him kings reign.</hi> He is present at all their debates, and inspects all they say and do, and what is said and done amiss will be called over again, and they reckoned with for their mal-administrations. God has their hearts in his hands, and their tongues too, and he directs them <hi type="italic">which way soever he will,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.21.1">Prov. xxi. 1</reference>. So that he has a negative voice in all their resolves, and his counsels shall stand, whatever devices are in men's hearts. He makes what use he pleases of them, and serves his own purposes and designs by them; though their hearts little think so, <reference osisRef="Isa.10.7">Isa. x. 7</reference>. Let magistrates consider this and be awed by it; God is with them in the judgment, <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.6">2 Chron. xix. 6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.1.17">Deut. i. 17</reference>. Let subjects consider this and be comforted with it; for good princes and good judges, who mean well, are under a divine direction, and bad ones, who mean ever so ill, are under a divine restraint. <div eID="gen11968" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11969" type="x-p"/> II. A charge given to all magistrates to do good with their power, as they will answer it to him by whom they are entrusted with it, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.3-Ps.82.4">v. 3, 4</reference>. 1. They are to be the protectors of those who lie exposed to injury and the patrons of those who want advice and assistance: <hi type="italic">Defend the poor,</hi> who have no money wherewith to make friends or fee counsel, <hi type="italic">and the fatherless,</hi> who, while they are young and unable to help themselves, have lost those who would have been the guides of their youth. Magistrates, as they must be fathers to their country in general, so particularly to those in it who are fatherless. Are they called <hi type="italic">gods?</hi> Herein they must be followers of him, they must be <hi type="italic">fathers of the fatherless.</hi> Job was so, <reference osisRef="Job.29.12">Job xxix. 12</reference>. 2. They are to administer justice impartially, and do <hi type="italic">right to the afflicted and needy,</hi> who, being weak and helpless, have often wrongs done them; and will be in danger of losing all if magistrates do not, <hi type="italic">ex officio—officially,</hi> interpose for their relief. If a poor man has an honest cause, his poverty must be no prejudice to his cause, how great and powerful soever those are that contend with him. 3. They are to rescue those who have already fallen into the hands of oppressors and deliver them. (<reference osisRef="Ps.82.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">Rid them out of the hand of the wicked. Avenge them of their adversary,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.18.3">Luke xviii. 3</reference>. These are clients whom there is nothing to be got by, no pay for serving them, no interest by obliging them; yet these are those whom judges and magistrates must concern themselves for, whose comfort they must consult and whose cause they must espouse. <div eID="gen11969" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11970" type="x-p"/> III. A charge drawn up against bad magistrates, who neglect their duty and abuse their power, forgetting that God standeth among them, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.2">v. 2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">5</reference>. Observe, 1. What the sin is they are here charged with; they <hi type="italic">judge unjustly,</hi> contrary to the rules of equity and the dictates of their consciences, giving judgment against those who have right on their side, out of malice and ill-will, or for those who have an unrighteous cause, out of favour and partial affection. To do unjustly is bad, but to judge unjustly is much worse, because it is doing wrong under colour of right; against such acts of injustice there is least fence for the injured and by them encouragement is given to the injurious. It was as great an evil as any Solomon saw under the sun when he observed <hi type="italic">the place of judgment, that iniquity was there,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Eccl. iii. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.5.7">Isa. v. 7</reference>. They not only accepted the persons of the rich because they were rich, though that is bad enough, but (which is much worse) they <hi type="italic">accepted the persons of the wicked</hi> because they were wicked; they not only countenanced them in their wickedness, but loved them the better for it, and fell in with their interests. Woe unto thee, O land! when thy judges are such as these. 2. What was the cause of this sin. They were told plainly enough that it was their office and duty to protect and deliver the poor; it was many a time given them in charge; yet they judge unjustly, for <hi type="italic">they know not, neither will they understand.</hi> They do not care to hear their duty; they will not take pains to study it; they have no desire to take things right, but are governed by interest, not by reason or justice. <hi type="italic">A gift in secret blinds their eyes.</hi> They know not because they will not understand. None so blind as those that will not see. They have baffled their own consciences, and so they walk on in darkness, not knowing nor caring what they do nor whither they go. Those that walk on in darkness are walking on to everlasting darkness. 3. What were the consequences of this sin: <hi type="italic">All the foundations of the earth</hi> (or <hi type="italic">of the land) are out of course.</hi> When justice is perverted what good can be expected? <hi type="italic">The earth and all the inhabitants thereof are dissolved,</hi> as the psalmist speaks in a like case, <reference osisRef="Ps.75.3">Ps. lxxv. 3</reference>. The miscarriages of public persons are public mischiefs.
entries.e972cc784db01a946e92aaafae9205f03dad47bf: <div eID="gen11970" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Duty of Magistrates.</title> <div sID="gen11971" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> I have said, Ye <hi type="italic">are</hi> gods; and all of you <hi type="italic">are</hi> children of the most High. <hi type="super">7</hi> But ye shall die like men, and fall like one of the princes. <hi type="super">8</hi> Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations. <div eID="gen11971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11972" type="x-p"/> We have here, <div eID="gen11972" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11973" type="x-p"/> I. Earthly gods abased and brought down, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.6-Ps.82.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. The dignity of their character is acknowledged (<reference osisRef="Ps.82.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">I have said, You are gods.</hi> They have been honoured with the name and title of gods. God himself called them so in the statute against treasonable words <reference osisRef="Exod.22.28">Exod. xxii. 28</reference>, <hi type="italic">Thou shalt not revile the gods.</hi> And, if they have this style from the fountain of honour, who can dispute it? But what is man, that he should be thus magnified? He called them <hi type="italic">gods</hi> because <hi type="italic">unto them the word of God came,</hi> so our Saviour expounds it (<reference osisRef="John.10.35">John x. 35</reference>); they had a commission from God, and were delegated and appointed by him to be the shields of the earth, the conservators of the public peace, and revengers to execute wrath upon those that disturb it, <reference osisRef="Rom.13.4">Rom. xiii. 4</reference>. All of them are in this sense <hi type="italic">children of the Most High.</hi> God has put some of his honour upon them, and employs them in his providential government of the world, as David made his sons chief rulers. Or, "Because <hi type="italic">I said, You are gods,</hi> you have carried the honour further than was intended and have imagined yourselves to be <hi type="italic">the children of the Most High,</hi>" as the king of Babylon (<reference osisRef="Isa.14.14">Isa. xiv. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will be like the Most High,</hi> and the king of Tyre (<reference osisRef="Ezek.28.2">Ezek. xxviii. 2</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thou hast set thy heart as the heart of God.</hi> It is a hard thing for men to have so much honour put upon them by the hand of God, and so much honour paid them, as ought to be by the children of men, and not to be proud of it and puffed up with it, and so to think of themselves above what is meet. But here follows a mortifying consideration: <hi type="italic">You shall die like men.</hi> This may be taken either, 1. As the punishment of bad magistrates, such as judged unjustly, and by their misrule put the <hi type="italic">foundations of the earth out of course.</hi> God will reckon with them, and will cut them off in the midst of their pomp and prosperity; they shall die like other wicked men, <hi type="italic">and fall like one of the</hi> heathen <hi type="italic">princes</hi> (and their being Israelites shall not secure them anymore than their being judges) or like one of the angels that sinned, or like one of the giants of the old world. Compare this with that which Elihu observed concerning the mighty oppressors in his time. <reference osisRef="Job.34.26">Job xxxiv. 26</reference>, <hi type="italic">He striketh them as wicked men in the open sight of others.</hi> Let those that abuse their power know that God will take both it and their lives from them; for wherein they deal proudly he will <hi type="italic">show himself above them.</hi> Or, 2. As the period of the glory of all magistrates in this world. Let them not be puffed up with their honour nor neglect their work, but let the consideration of their mortality be both mortifying to their pride and quickening to their duty. "You are called gods, but you have no patent for immortality; <hi type="italic">you shall die like men,</hi> like common men; and <hi type="italic">like one of them, you, O princes! shall fall.</hi>" Note, Kings and princes, all the judges of the earth, though they are gods to us, are men to God, and shall die like men, and all their honour shall be laid in the dust. <hi type="italic">Mors sceptra ligonibus æquat—Death mingles sceptres with spades.</hi> <div eID="gen11973" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11974" type="x-p"/> II. The God of heaven exalted and raised high, <reference osisRef="Ps.82.8">v. 8</reference>. The psalmist finds it to little purpose to reason with these proud oppressors; they turned a deaf ear to all he said and walked on in darkness; and therefore he looks up to God, appeals to him, and begs of him <hi type="italic">to take unto himself his great power: Arise, O God! judge the earth;</hi> and, when he prays that he would do it, he believes that he will do it: <hi type="italic">Thou shalt inherit all nations.</hi> This has respect, 1. To the kingdom of providence. God governs the world, sets up and puts down whom he pleases; he inherits all nations, has an absolute dominion over them, to dispose of them as a man does of his inheritance. This we are to believe and to comfort ourselves with, that the earth is not given so much <hi type="italic">into the hands of the wicked,</hi> the wicked rulers, as we are tempted to think it is, <reference osisRef="Job.9.24">Job ix. 24</reference>. But God has reserved the power to himself and overrules them. In this faith we must pray, "<hi type="italic">Arise, O God! judge the earth,</hi> appear against those that judge unjustly, and set shepherds over thy people after thy own heart." There is a righteous God to whom we may have recourse, and on whom we may depend for the effectual relief of all that find themselves aggrieved by unjust judges. 2. To the kingdom of the Messiah. It is a prayer for the hastening of that, that Christ would come, who is to judge the earth, and that promise is pleaded, that God shall <hi type="italic">give him the heathen for his inheritance.</hi> Thou, O Christ! shalt <hi type="italic">inherit all nations,</hi> and be the governor over them, <reference osisRef="Ps.2.8">Ps. ii. 8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.22.28">xxii. 28</reference>. Let the second coming of Christ set to-rights all these disorders. There are two words with which we may comfort ourselves and one another in reference to the mismanagements of power among men: one is <reference osisRef="Rev.19.6">Rev. xix. 6</reference>, <hi type="italic">Hallelujah, the Lord God omnipotent reigneth;</hi> the other is <reference osisRef="Rev.22.20">Rev. xxii. 20</reference>, <hi type="italic">Surely, I come quickly.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ps.82"/> <div eID="gen11974" type="x-p"/>

entries.a7e23f76acb58a6441256be23289895c1d82b118: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6454"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 82</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.82.1-Ps.82.8">Psa 82:1-8</reference>. Before the great Judge, the judges of the earth are rebuked, exhorted, and threatened.</title> <div sID="gen9890" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6454"/><hi type="bold">1. congregation--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Exod.12.3">Ex 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.16.1">16:1</reference>).<div eID="gen9890" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9891" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the mighty--</hi>that is, of God, of His appointment.<div eID="gen9891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9892" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the gods--</hi>or, "judges" (<reference osisRef="Exod.21.6">Ex 21:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.22.9">22:9</reference>), God's representatives. <div eID="gen9892" type="x-p"/>
entries.0c0ea872a88b5927a2dd248dbcc732ac947d49bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6455"/><div sID="gen9893" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6455"/><hi type="bold">2. accept the persons--</hi>literally, "lift up the faces," that is, from dejection, or admit to favor and communion, regardless of merit (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.15">Le 19:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.18.5">Pr 18:5</reference>). <div eID="gen9893" type="x-p"/>
entries.edeeb3efb441f1adedc3419c7f3152bbb0cdec69: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6456"/><div sID="gen9894" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6456"/>3-4. So must good judges act (<reference osisRef="Ps.10.14">Psa 10:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.29.12">Job 29:12</reference>). <div eID="gen9894" type="x-p"/>
entries.ebb1f61935fe028638d6fb41c1e88834af1bbbff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6458"/><div sID="gen9896" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6458"/>5. By the wilful ignorance and negligence of judges, anarchy ensues (<reference osisRef="Ps.11.3">Psa 11:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.75.3">75:3</reference>).<div eID="gen9896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9897" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">out of course--</hi>(Compare Margin; <reference osisRef="Ps.9.6">Psa 9:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.62.2">62:2</reference>). <div eID="gen9897" type="x-p"/>
entries.3e0fbe28a6d1eb60639f57412e9311a23554f9c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6459"/><div sID="gen9898" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6459"/>6-7. Though God admitted their official dignity (<reference osisRef="John.10.34">Joh 10:34</reference>), He reminds them of their mortality. <div eID="gen9898" type="x-p"/>
entries.5bc019d885aea1b4b8775391667b4251a20f72a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6461"/><div sID="gen9900" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6461"/>8. As rightful sovereign of earth, God is invoked personally to correct the evils of His representatives. <chapter eID="Ps.82"/>

entries.b881b1432d4f6e016f70a040599e725387cf4f47: <div eID="gen21268" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen21269" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21270" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21270" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen21269" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen21271" type="x-p"/> A warning to corrupt judges, <reference osisRef="Psa.82.1">Psa 82:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="Psa.82.2">Psa 82:2</reference>; an exhortation to them to dispense justice without respect of person, <reference osisRef="Psa.82.3-Psa.82.5">Psa 82:3-5</reference>; they are threatened with the judgments of the Lord, <reference osisRef="Psa.82.6-Psa.82.8">Psa 82:6-8</reference>. <div eID="gen21271" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21272" type="x-p"/> This Psalm, which, in the title, is attributed to Asaph, was probably composed in the time when Jehoshaphat reformed the courts of justice throughout his states; see <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.6">2Chr 19:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.19.7">2Chr 19:7</reference>, where he uses nearly the same words as in the beginning of this Psalm. <div eID="gen21272" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21273" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen21273" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21274" type="x-p"/> God standeth in the congregation of the mighty - The Hebrew should be translated, "God standeth in the assembly of God." God is among his people; and he presides especially in those courts of justice which himself has established. The Court of King's Bench is properly the place where the king presides, and where he is supposed to be always present. But the kings of England seldom make their appearance there. King James I sometimes attended: at such times it might be said, "The king is in the king's court." I believe the case above to be similar. Judges! beware what you do! God is in his court, and in the midst (of the assembly) God will judge. See Parkhurst under אלה.
entries.4ca603877f1dcf42fe42cb99502aa620d1f4f141: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen21274" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21275" type="x-p"/> Accept the persons of the wicked? - "Lift up their faces," encourage them in their oppressions. <div eID="gen21275" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21276" type="x-p"/> Selah - "Mark this:" ye do it, and sorely sLall ye suffer for it.
entries.03b834a68e6c91890598864e530ae0f0bb7fef0c: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen21276" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21277" type="x-p"/> Defend the poor - You are their natural protectors under God. They are oppressed: punish their oppressors, however rich or powerful: and deliver them.
entries.e48c74d187180378cd77609dce7f5f2ff29b7ae8: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen21277" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21278" type="x-p"/> They know not - The judges are not acquainted with the law of God, on which all their decisions should be founded. <div eID="gen21278" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21279" type="x-p"/> Neither will they understand - They are ignorant and do not wish to be instructed. They will not learn; they cannot teach. Happy England! How different from Judea, even in the days of Jehoshaphat! All thy judges are learned, righteous, and impartial. Never did greater men in their profession dignify any land or country - (1822). <div eID="gen21279" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21280" type="x-p"/> All the foundations of the earth - "All the civil institutions of the land totter." Justice is at the head of all the institutions in a well regulated state: when that gets poisoned or perverted, every evil, political and domestic, must prevail; even religion itself ceases to have any influence.
entries.35b3f516e46ea331cfce41837c15975991d178ee: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen21280" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21281" type="x-p"/> Ye are gods - Or, with the prefix of כ ke, the particle of similitude, כאלהים keelohim, "like God." Ye are my representatives, and are clothed with my power and authority to dispense judgment and justice, therefore all of them are said to be children of the Most High.
entries.0206c058b6fee70b2960acd44430c79ceb7ccdb7: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen21281" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21282" type="x-p"/> But ye shall die like men - כאדם keadam, "ye shall die like Adam," who fell from his high perfection and dignity as ye have done. Your high office cannot secure you an immortality. <div eID="gen21282" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21283" type="x-p"/> And fall like one of the princes - Justice shall pursue you, and judgment shall overtake you; and you shall be executed like public state criminals. You shall not, in the course of nature, fall into the grave; but your life shall be brought to an end by a legal sentence, or a particular judgment of God.
entries.337275268ef028e2c2d9e1b121e9c88d479dfd9b: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen21283" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21284" type="x-p"/> Arise, O God, judge the earth - Justice is perverted in the land: take the scepter, and rule thyself. <div eID="gen21284" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen21285" type="x-p"/> For thou shalt inherit all nations - Does not this last verse contain a prophecy of our Lord, the calling of the Gentiles, and the prevalence of Christianity over the earth? Thus several of the fathers have understood the passage. It is only by the universal spread of Christianity over the world, that the reign of righteousness and justice is to be established: and of whom can it be said that he shall inherit all nations, but of Jesus Christ?  <chapter eID="Ps.82"/> <div eID="gen21285" type="x-p"/>

entries.ccd9733a0a34f8711acd8772fb7ee567d823a532: <reference osisRef="Ps.82.1-Ps.82.4">Psa 82:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen9837" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9838" type="x-p"/> God comes forward and makes Himself heard first of all as censuring and admonishing. The “congregation of God” is, as in Num 27:17; Num 31:16; Jos 22:16., “the congregation of (the sons of) Israel,” which God has purchased from among the nations (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.2">Psa 74:2</reference>), and upon which as its Lawgiver He has set His divine impress. The psalmist and seer sees Elohim standing in this congregation of God. The <hi type="italic">part.</hi> <hi type="italic">Niph</hi>. (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.3.13">Isa 3:13</reference>) denotes not so much the suddenness and unpreparedness, as, rather, the statue-like immobility and terrifying designfulness of His appearance. Within the range of the congregation of God this holds good of the <hi type="italic">elohim</hi>. The right over life and death, with which the administration of justice cannot dispense, is a prerogative of God. From the time of <reference osisRef="Gen.9.6">Gen 9:6</reference>, however, He has transferred the execution of this prerogative to mankind, and instituted in mankind an office wielding the sword of justice, which also exists in His theocratic congregation, but here has His positive law as the basis of its continuance and as the rule of its action. Everywhere among men, but here pre-eminently, those in authority are God’s delegates and the bearers of His image, and therefore as His representatives are also themselves called <hi type="italic">elohim</hi>, “gods” (which the lxx in <reference osisRef="Exod.21.6">Exo 21:6</reference> renders τὸ κριτήριον τοῦ Θεοῦ, and the Targums here, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.22.7-Exod.22.8">Exo 22:7-8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.22.27">Exo 22:27</reference> uniformly, דּיּניּא). The God who has conferred this exercise of power upon these subordinate elohim, without their resigning it of themselves, now sits in judgment in their midst. ישׁפּט of that which takes place before the mind’s eye of the psalmist. How long, He asks, will ye judge unjustly? שׁפט עול is equivalent to עשׂה עול בּמּשׁפּט, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.15">Lev 19:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.19.35">Lev 19:35</reference> (the opposite is שׁפט מישׁרים, <reference osisRef="Ps.58.2">Psa 58:2</reference>). How long will ye accept the countenance of the wicked, i.e., incline to accept, regard, favour the person of the wicked? The music, which here becomes <hi type="italic">forte</hi>, gives intensity to the terrible sternness (<hi type="italic">das Niederdonnernde</hi>) of the divine question, which seeks to bring the “gods” of the earth to their right mind. Then follow admonitions to do that which they have hitherto left undone. They are to cause the benefit of the administration of justice to tend to the advantage of the defenceless, of the destitute, and of the helpless, upon whom God the Lawgiver especially keeps His eye. The word רשׁ (ראשׁ), of which there is no evidence until within the time of David and Solomon, is synonymous with אביון. דל with ויתום is pointed דל, and with ואביון, on account of the closer notional union, דל (as in <reference osisRef="Ps.72.13">Psa 72:13</reference>). They are words which are frequently repeated in the prophets, foremost in Isaiah (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.17">Isa 1:17</reference>), with which is enjoined upon those invested with the dignity of the law, and with jurisdiction, justice towards those who cannot and will not themselves obtain their rights by violence.
entries.0bd0a75162fd34307611ae374533c48554b4f1c9: <reference osisRef="Ps.82.5-Ps.82.7">Psa 82:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen9838" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9839" type="x-p"/> What now follows in <reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">Psa 82:5</reference> is not a parenthetical assertion of the inefficiency with which the divine correction rebounds from the judges and rulers. In connection with this way of taking <reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">Psa 82:5</reference>, the manner in which the divine language is continued in <reference osisRef="Ps.82.6">Psa 82:6</reference> is harsh and unadjusted. God Himself speaks in <reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">Psa 82:5</reference> of the judges, but reluctantly alienated from them; and confident of the futility of all attempts to make them better, He tells them their sentence in Psa 82:6. The verbs in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.82.5">Psa 82:5</reference></hi> are designedly without any object: complaint of the widest compass is made over their want of reason and understanding; and ידעו takes the perfect form in like manner to ἐγνώκασι, <hi type="italic">noverunt</hi>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.14.1">Psa 14:1</reference>; Isa 44:18. Thus, then, no result is to be expected from the divine admonition: they still go their ways in this state of mental darkness, and that, as the <hi type="italic">Hithpa</hi>. implies, stalking on in carnal security and self-complacency. The commands, however, which they transgress are the foundations (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.11.3">Psa 11:3</reference>), as it were the shafts and pillars (<reference osisRef="Ps.75.4">Psa 75:4</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.29.4">Pro 29:4</reference>), upon which rests the permanence of all earthly relationships with are appointed by creation and regulated by the Tôra. Their transgression makes the land, the earth, to totter physically and morally, and is the prelude of its overthrow. When the celestial Lord of the domain thinks upon this destruction which injustice and tyranny are bringing upon the earth, His wrath kindles, and He reminds the judges and rulers that it is His own free declaratory act which has clothed them with the god-like dignity which they bear. They are actually elohim, but not possessed of the right of self-government; there is a Most High (עליון) to whom they as sons are responsible. The idea that the appellation <hi type="italic">elohim</hi>, which they have given to themselves, is only sarcastically given back to them in <reference osisRef="Ps.82.1">Psa 82:1</reference> (Ewald, Olshausen), is refuted by <reference osisRef="Ps.82.6">Psa 82:6</reference>, according to which they are really <hi type="italic">elohim</hi> by the grace of God. But if their practice is not an Amen to this name, then they shall be divested of the majesty which they have forfeited; they shall be divested of the prerogative of Israel, whose vocation and destiny they have belied. They shall die off כּאדם, like common men not rising in any degree above the mass (cf. בּני אדם, <hi type="italic">opp</hi>. בּני אישׁ, <reference osisRef="Ps.4.3">Psa 4:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.49.3">Psa 49:3</reference>); they shall fall like any one (Jdg 16:7, Oba 1:11) of the princes who in the course of history have been cast down by the judgment of God (Hos 7:7). Their divine office will not protect them. For although <hi type="italic">justitia civilis</hi> is far from being the righteousness that avails before God, yet <hi type="italic">injustitia civilis</hi> is in His sight the vilest abomination.
entries.3b172808ecdbafcaa366951b6f8f3c8cac4edc3a: <reference osisRef="Ps.82.8">Psa 82:8</reference> <div eID="gen9839" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9840" type="x-p"/> The poet closes with the prayer for the realization of that which he has beheld in spirit. He implored God Himself to sit in judgment (שׁפטה as in <reference osisRef="Lam.3.59">Lam 3:59</reference>), since judgment is so badly exercised upon the earth. All peoples are indeed His נחלה, He has an hereditary and proprietary right among (lxx and Vulgate according to Num 18:20, and frequently), or rather in (בּ as in משׁל בּ, instead of the accusative of the object, Zec 2:11), all nations (ἔθνη) - may He then be pleased to maintain it judicially. The inference drawn from this point backwards, that the Psalm is directed against the possessors of power among the Gentiles, is erroneous. Israel itself, in so far as it acts inconsistently with its theocratic character, belies its sanctified nationality, is a גוי like the גוים, and is put into the same category with these. The judgment over the world is also a judgment over the Israel that is become conformed to the world, and its God-estranged chiefs.  <chapter eID="Ps.82"/> <div eID="gen9840" type="x-p"/>

entries.531b8c7acfb452d7ff0026fffbfab0ee6d3a5d5c:
PSALM 82
As kings, and such as are invested with authority, through the blindness which is produced by pride, generally take to themselves a boundless liberty of action, the Psalmist warns them that they must render an account at the bar of the Supreme Judge, who is exalted above the highest of this world. After he has reminded them of their duty and condition, perceiving that he speaks to such as refuse to receive admonition, he calls upon God to vindicate his character as a righteous judge.
Kimchi thinks it probable that this psalm was written in the days of Jehoshaphat, and refers to 2 Chronicles 19:5-7, as indicating the time and occasion of its composition. We are there informed that Jehoshaphat; “set judges in the land, throughout all the fenced cities of Judah, city by city;” and in instructing them with regard to their duty, he uses nearly the same words as those in the beginning of this psalm. Dr Morison takes a different view. “This psalm,” says he, “was composed in all probability in the days of Hezekiah, in reference to certain wicked magistrates, (2 Chronicles 29:30,) who had grievously perverted the administration of justice, who were guilty of great oppression, and who had done much to introduce a state of general national corruption. King Jehoshaphat had reformed several public abuses which had crept into the judicatories of Israel in his time, (2 Chronicles 19:7,) but before the reign of Hezekiah, things had reverted to their former unhappy condition; so that a public national reformation was loudly demanded. The psalm contains an exhortation to the judges of Israel, and a reproof for their negligence and oppression.”
A Psalm of Asaph.
Psalm 82:1-4
1. God sitteth in the assembly of God: he will judge in the midst of the gods.
“Ou, il jugeras au milieu les dieux.” — Fr. marg. “Or, he will judge in the midst the gods.”
2. How long will ye judge unjustly? and accept the persons of the wicked? Selah. 3. Determine the cause of the poor and the orphan; justify
“C’est, faites justice.” — Fr. marg. “That is, do justice to.”
the helpless and the destitute. 4. Rescue the poor and the afflicted: deliver them out of the hand of the wicked.
 
1 God sitteth in the assembly of God.
Horsley translates the first verse thus: —
“God standeth in the assembly; God, in the midst of the gods, giveth sentence.”
On which he has the following note: — “In what assembly? The assembly of his holy angels. The Psalmist, I think, poetically imagines the celestial court assembled for the business of this review of the proceedings of the earth’s judges, and God, in the midst of his angels, taxing their iniquity, and awarding their punishment.”
It is unquestionably a very unbecoming thing for those whom God has been pleased to invest with the government of mankind for the common good, not to acknowledge the end for which they have been exalted above others, nor yet by whose blessing they have been placed in so elevated a station; but instead of doing this, contemning every principle of equity, to rule just as their own unbridled passions dictate. So infatuated are they by their own splendor and magnificence, as to imagine that the whole world was made only for them. Besides, they think that it would derogate from their elevated rank were they to be governed by moderate counsels; and although their own folly is more than enough to urge them on in their reckless career, they, notwithstanding, seek for flatterers to soothe and applaud them in their vices. To correct this arrogance, the psalm opens by asserting, that although men occupy thrones and judgment-seats, God nevertheless continues to hold the office of supreme ruler. God has made even a heathen and licentious poet bear testimony to this truth in the following lines: —
“Regum timendorum in proprios greges, Reges in ipsos imperium est Jovis, Clari giganteo triumpho, Cuncta supercilio moventis.” Horatii, Carm. Liber in Ode i.
“Kings rule their subject flocks; great Jove O’er kings themselves his reign extends, Who hurl’d the rebel giants from above; At whose majestic nod all nature bends.” Boscawen’s Translation.
That the potentates of this world may not arrogate to themselves more than belongs to them, the prophet here erects a throne for God, from which he judges them all, and represses their pride; a thing which is highly necessary. They may, indeed, admit that they owe their elevation to royal power to the favor of God, and they may worship him by outward ceremonies, but their greatness so infatuates them that they are chargeable with expelling and casting him to a distance from their assembly, by their vain imaginations; for they cannot bear to be subject to reason and laws. Thus the design of the prophet was to deride the madness by which the princes of this world are bewitched, in leaving God no place in their assembly. The more effectually to overthrow this irrational self-confidence with which they are intoxicated, civil order is termed the assembly of God; for although the divine glory shines forth in every part of the world, yet when lawful government flourishes among men, it is reflected therefrom with pre-eminent lustre. I indeed grant that it is quite common for the Hebrews to adorn with the title of God whatever is rare and excellent. But here it would appear, from the scope of the passage, that this name of the Divine Being is applied to those who occupy the exalted station of princes, in which there is afforded a peculiar manifestation of the majesty of God; even as Solomon, in Proverbs 2:17, calls marriage “the covenant of God,” from the peculiar sanctity by which that relation is distinguished.
In the second clause of the verse, it is not material whether we read, He will judge in the midst of the gods, or, He will judge the gods in the midst. The first construction, however, is the most easy and natural, That however much the rulers of the world may exalt themselves, they cannot in the least impair the authority of God, by divesting him of his sovereignty over them and of the government of all things, which he will ever retain as his inalienable prerogative. But here, as also a little after, the name gods is to be understood of judges, on whom God has impressed special marks of his glory. To apply it to angels is a fancy too strained to admit of serious consideration.

                     <ns0:p>This <ns0:hi>Psalm</ns0:hi> contains an Admonition either 1. To the chief Rulers of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> whether Iudges or Kings, or their great Council called the <ns0:hi>Sanhe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />drim.</ns0:hi> Or rather, 2. To all the Rulers of the several Nations of the World, to whom this word might come? as may be gathered partly from the expressions here used, which are general and not peculiar to the Governors of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> and there<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fore not rashly and unnecessarily to be restrained; and partly from the last Verse, where he mentions the whole <ns0:hi>earth</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>all nations,</ns0:hi> as concerned in the Contents of this <ns0:hi>Psalm.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="1">1 GOd standeth <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">As a Judge diligently to observe all that is said or one there; and to give sentence accordingly. The Judge sits when he heareth Causes, but standeth up when he giveth sentence. Or <ns0:hi>standing</ns0:hi> doth not note the posture; but onely the being or presence of a person, as <ns0:hi>Isa.</ns0:hi> 11. 10. <ns0:hi>Dan.</ns0:hi> 11. 10. <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 3. 29. Whence this Hebrew Word is by some Learned Interpreters rendred <ns0:hi>is present,</ns0:hi> and by others, <ns0:hi>presideth,</ns0:hi> as this word is used, 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 19. 20. <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> 22. 9.</ns0:note> in the congregation of <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb. <ns0:hi>God.</ns0:hi> Psal. 89. 7. <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> 95. 3.</ns0:note> the mighty <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>of the gods,</ns0:hi> as it is explained and expressed in the next Clause; the sin<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gular number being here, as it is frequently elsewhere, put for the plural. By <ns0:hi>Gods,</ns0:hi> or the <ns0:hi>mighty,</ns0:hi> he understands Kings, or other chief Rulers, who are so called because they have their power and commission from God, and act as his Deputies in his name and stead, and must give an account to him of all their Actions. And by their <ns0:hi>congregation</ns0:hi> he understands not a convention or assembly of such persons which seldom meet together, but either 1. All Congregations or Assemblies of People in which Magistrates sit to execute Justice. Or 2. All persons whatsoever of this high and sacred Order or Number: for the Hebrew Word here rendred <ns0:hi>congregation,</ns0:hi> doth not always signifie an Assembly of persons met toge<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther in one place, but sometimes notes all the particular per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sons of or belonging to such a sort and body of men, though dispersed in divers places, as <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 26. 5. <ns0:hi>I have hated the con<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />gregtion of evil doers (i. e.)</ns0:hi> all evil doers. <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 21. 16. he <ns0:hi>shall remain in the congregation of the dead, (i. e.)</ns0:hi> shall be one of that number and state. See also <ns0:hi>Ios.</ns0:hi> 22. 20. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 74. 19. Some render it as it is in the Hebrew, <ns0:hi>in the congregation of God,</ns0:hi> in his own Congregation, the Noun being put for the Pronoun, as is usual in the Hebrew Text, (<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) in the Conventions or Tribunals of Princes or Rulers, which he rightly calls <ns0:hi>his,</ns0:hi> because their authority is wholly derived from him. But the former Exposition seems more agreeable both to the following words, and to the scope and whole Body of the Psalm.</ns0:note>: he judgeth <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">Accurately observeth all their carriages, and passeth sentence upon them accordingly.</ns0:note> among the gods <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">(<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) Judges and Magistrates, who are called <ns0:hi>gods</ns0:hi> below, <ns0:hi>Verse</ns0:hi> 6. and <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 12. 12. <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> 22. 28. compared with <ns0:hi>Act.</ns0:hi> 23. 5. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 138. 1. and of whom this is expounded, <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 10. 34, 35.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2 How long will ye judge unjustly <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">The Psalmist speaketh to them in God's name, and re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proves them for their continued and resolved unrighteousness in their publick Administrations.</ns0:note>, and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Deut. 1. 17: 2 Chron. 19. 7.</ns0:note> ac<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cept the persons <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">By over-looking the me<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rits of the cause, and giving sentence according to your re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />spect or affection to the person.</ns0:note> of the wicked! Selah.</ns0:p>

                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> Iudg.</ns0:note> Defend the poor and fatherless <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">So far as justly you may; as this Clause must be limi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted by comparing this with <ns0:hi>Levit.</ns0:hi> 19. 15.</ns0:note>: do justice to <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">Heb. <ns0:hi>Iustifie,</ns0:hi> to wit, when his cause is just, and he is oppressed by a po<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tent Adversary.</ns0:note> the afflicted and needy.</ns0:p>

                  <ns0:p n="5">5 They <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The Magistrates of whom this Psalm treats.</ns0:note> know not <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">To wit, the truth and right of the cause, nor the duty of their place. Men are oft said in Scripture <ns0:hi>not to know</ns0:hi> what they do not love and practise.</ns0:note>, neither will they un<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />derstand <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">This their ignorance is willful and af<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fected: they will not search out the truth, and they shut their eyes lest they should see what they would not.</ns0:note>; they walk on <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">They per<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sist and proceed: it is not one rash and transient action, but their constant course.</ns0:note> in darkness <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Either 1. In ignorance, or 2. In their sinful and unrighteous courses, as <ns0:hi>darkness</ns0:hi> is taken <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 4. 17, 18 <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> 5. 8. 1 <ns0:hi>Ioh.</ns0:hi> 1. 6. Being blinded by their cor<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rupt affections and interests, <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 23. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">

                        </ns0:gap>.</ns0:note>: all the foundations of the earth are <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> moved.</ns0:note> out of course <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">This corruption of the supreme Rulers doth flow from them to their inferior Officers and Members, and manifestly tends to the dissolution of all civil Societies, partly by subverting that order and ho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nesty by which they are supported; and partly by provoking God the Governor of the world to destroy them for their wickedness.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">John 10. 34.</ns0:note> I have said, Ye <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> gods <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">I have given you my name and power to rule your peo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple in my stead.</ns0:note>: and all of you <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">Not onely the Rulers of <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> but of all other Nations; <ns0:hi>for all powers are ordained by God,</ns0:hi> Rom. 13. 1.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> children of the most High <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">Representing my person, and bearing both my name and lively characters of my Majesty and Authority, as <ns0:hi>children</ns0:hi> bear the name and image of their Parents.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7. But ye shall die <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">But let not this make you insolent and secure; for though you are <ns0:hi>gods</ns0:hi> by name and office, yet still you are mortal men, you must die and give up your account to me your superior Lord and Governor; and you shall die and fall by the hands of my Justice, if you persist in your unjust and ungodly courses.</ns0:note> like men <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>like ordinary men,</ns0:hi> as the Hebrew word, <ns0:hi>Adam,</ns0:hi> sometimes signifies, as it doth <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 49. 2. If it be objected, that there <ns0:hi>Adam</ns0:hi> is opposed to <ns0:hi>I<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>h,</ns0:hi> which notes persons of an higher rank; in like manner it is here opposed to the same sort of men, who are here called <ns0:hi>gods.</ns0:hi>
                     </ns0:note>, and fall like one of the princes <ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">So the sence is, <ns0:hi>You</ns0:hi> (who are esteemed by your selves and others, gods upon earth) <ns0:hi>shall fall,</ns0:hi> (or <ns0:hi>die,</ns0:hi> as he said in the former branch: <ns0:hi>falling</ns0:hi> being oft put for dying, with this ad<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dition that it notes not an ordinary, but a violent and ju<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dicial death, as <ns0:hi>Exod.</ns0:hi> 19. 21. <ns0:hi>Ier.</ns0:hi> 39. 18. <ns0:hi>Hos.</ns0:hi> 5. 5.) <ns0:hi>like one</ns0:hi> (or, <ns0:hi>like other,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>others,</ns0:hi> as this very word is rendred, <ns0:hi>Iudg.</ns0:hi> 16. 7, 11. which also is expounded there, <ns0:hi>Verse</ns0:hi> 17. <ns0:hi>like every</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>any) of the princes (i. e.)</ns0:hi> as other unrighteous or tyrannical Rulers have done in all foregoing Ages, and still do, your eyes seeing it; even in like manner shall you, to whom now I speak, fall and perish, if you do not learn by their Examples. But these words are by some late Learned Inter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />preters translated otherwise, and that very agreeably to the Hebrew words and accents, <ns0:hi>And</ns0:hi> you, <ns0:hi>O ye princes</ns0:hi> (or, you <ns0:hi>that are princes,</ns0:hi> before called <ns0:hi>gods) shall fall like one</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>like every</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> of them, (<ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi>) of the ordinary men last menti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />oned. So there is onely an <ns0:hi>Ellipsis</ns0:hi> of the Pronoun, which is frequent in the Hebrew Language. Or, <ns0:hi>shall fall together,</ns0:hi> as this word is translated, <ns0:hi>Ezra</ns0:hi> 2. 64. <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> 3. 9. or <ns0:hi>alike,</ns0:hi> as it is rendred, <ns0:hi>Eccles.</ns0:hi> 11. 6. <ns0:hi>in like manner,</ns0:hi> to wit, as ordinary men do. Your god-head shall be taken away from you, and your death shall shew you to be but mortal men as others are.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8 Arise, O God, judge the earth <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">Seeing the state of the world is so universally corrupt and desperate, and thy Vicegerents betray their trust, and oppress and ruine the Nations of the earth, whom they were appoint<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ed to preserve, do thou therefore, O God, take the sword of Justice into thine own hand, and maintain the cause and rights of the oppressed against their potent Oppressors, and let truth and justice be established in all the parts of the earth. For as thou wast the Creator, so thou still art the supreme and unquestionable Lord and Possessor and Ruler of all Nations, and therefore do thou protect and rescue them from all those who invade thine and their rights. And although at present thou seemest in some sort to confine thy care to <ns0:hi>Israel,</ns0:hi> and to neglect other Nations, yet there is a time coming when thou wilt bring all Nations to the knowledge of thy self, and the obedience of thy Laws, and govern them by thy Son and Spirit which thou wilt send into the world for that purpose. Do thou therefore preserve them in the mean time till that blessed day cometh, and hasten the coming of it.</ns0:note>, for thou shalt inherit all nations <ns0:hi>z.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:p>
               </ns0:div>
